title: Typeset: Typewriter and Handwriting Text Sounds
shortText: 143 typewriter, teletype, terminal, quill, pencil and chalk text sounds for dialogue boxes. WAV + OGG.
html:
Typewriter and handwriting text sounds

143 text sounds for dialogue that is written rather than spoken. 11 writing voices, each with the same 13 cues a text box can drive.

A dialogue box, a terminal log, a letter, a diary page or a classroom board can sound like the thing writing the words: a manual typewriter, a teletype, a green screen terminal, a telegraph sounder, a quill, a pencil or a stick of chalk. Every voice ships six takes for each typed character plus its own word gap, line end, page, open, close, emphasis and correction, so a text system wired for one voice takes any other by changing one word.

Licence, up front

Royalty free. Commercial use. No credit required. No revenue limit, no unit cap, no second licence to buy later if your game does well. Use it in as many projects as you like, on any platform. The one thing you may not do is resell the sounds themselves as sounds. The full plain language terms ship as LICENSE.txt, with a copy paste credit line if you want one.

Everything is synthesised from code. No recordings, no sample libraries, no third party clips, so there is no upstream licence behind this one and nobody can content ID claim these sounds against your project.

Hear it first

There is a free demo on this page: 47 sounds, the first character take of every one of the 11 voices plus three voices complete with all their cues, copied unaltered from the paid files. Play the eleven character sounds back to back before you pay.

6 machines

  • Manual Typewriter. A steel typebar striking a rubber platen through paper, with the key falling back after it. 2961 Hz, 62 ms
  • Electric Typewriter. A golf ball element snapped onto the page by a solenoid: tighter and quicker than the manual. 2928 Hz, 40 ms
  • Teletype. A five unit code clicking through the selector magnet, then the print hammer. Each take is a real letter code. 2608 Hz, 136 ms
  • Green Screen Terminal. A terminal keyclick from a tiny speaker: the shortest voice here. 4385 Hz, 16 ms
  • Dot Matrix Printer. Columns of print needles firing across one glyph. Each take is a different letter shape. 4414 Hz, 28 ms
  • Telegraph Sounder. A sounder armature clicking down and clacking back up: a dot or a dash per character. 2255 Hz, 139 ms

5 hands

  • Pencil. Graphite dragged across paper: a short gritty stroke with a soft tap where the tip lands. 6025 Hz, 80 ms
  • Dip Pen. A steel nib on paper: thin, scratchy, with the point catching on the fibres. 8086 Hz, 59 ms
  • Quill. A cut quill on parchment: softer and airier than a steel nib, with the feather brushing along. 4507 Hz, 112 ms
  • Chalk. Chalk on a slate board: a hard tap where it lands, then a gritty dragged stroke. 5410 Hz, 109 ms
  • Felt Marker. A felt tip gliding wet and smooth: the darkest voice here. 1953 Hz, 94 ms

Figures are the mean brightness and length of each voice's six character takes, measured off the shipped WAV files. All 55 pairs of voices are separated by at least 12 percent in brightness or 25 percent in length, and the comparisons in the descriptions above (the darkest, the shortest, quicker, softer) are checked against those measurements before the files are written: 7 of 7 hold.

The cues

  • char_01 to char_06. One per typed character; play a random one of the six.
  • space. the word gap: play it on a space instead of a character.
  • line. line end: play it when the text wraps or a new line starts.
  • page. page or paragraph: play it when the box clears for the next page.
  • open. the dialogue box opens.
  • close. the dialogue box closes.
  • emphasis. a bold, shouted or underlined word.
  • error. a correction: a struck out word, a backspace, an erasure.

Each cue is the voice's own mechanism: the typewriter rings its margin bell and throws the carriage back, the teletype sends its carriage return and line feed codes, the quill is dipped in a clay inkwell, the telegraph sounds the real new paragraph signal. The teletype's six character takes are six real letter codes and the dot matrix printer's are six different glyphs.

Fit

  • WAV and OGG for every file, 16 bit, 44.1 kHz, mono. File names are voice then cue.
  • Crawl speed is in the Readme. For every voice, the fastest text crawl at which one sound per character does not

overlap itself, from 7 to 62 characters a second. Above it, play one every second or third character.

  • One loudness band. The inner 80 percent of the pack sits inside 1.57 dB, so switching voice or cue never changes

how loud the text box is.

  • 11 declared variation sets, six takes per voice, differing in length and in brightness.
  • Nothing loops, and no file carries loop points. Checked in a blank Godot 4 project: every file imports and loads with

the default settings.

  • pack_proof.json ships with the pack: 1296 checks, 0 failed.

Honest limits

These are synthesised writing sounds, not recordings of real machines. The letter codes, glyphs and telegraph signals are authored to be true to the originals; the sound of each is a model. The measurements above are signal measurements, not a claim that it sounds good. That is what the free demo is for.

AI disclosure, stated truthfully: the code that generates these sounds was written with AI assistance. The sounds themselves are self contained procedural synthesis, resonators, filters, noise and envelopes evaluated in code, with no generative audio model at any point. The cover art and store graphics are AI generated.
